notes: The heading can mean a song by, for, or associated with Solomon. “Song of songs” is a Hebrew way of marking an outstanding song.
The Hebrew joins “black” and “beautiful” with “and.” It need not make beauty an exception to her skin color.
The difficult expression is often understood as “veiled,” though “wandering” is also possible. The precise social implication is unstated.
vocabulary: A female horse. The comparison places her among Pharaoh’s impressive chariots.

notes: The precise flowers are uncertain. The familiar English plant names are approximate identifications, not botanical certainty.
The oath invokes gazelles and does and leaves love’s timing to love itself. Speaker labels throughout this reader are editorial aids, guided by grammar; the Hebrew supplies no cast list.
The word can refer to singing or pruning. The surrounding lines evoke the sounds and growth of spring.
The day “breathing” and shadows fleeing can be heard as dawn or evening. Bether may be a place name or evoke divided, cleft mountains.
vocabulary: A conspicuous standard; here an image of love. The phrase has also been understood in terms of his intention toward her.

notes: The feminine question can be heard as “Who is this?” or “What is this?” The following procession does not settle every detail of the scene.
The description of the interior as worked with love is compressed and unusual; exactly how the daughters of Jerusalem relate to that workmanship is uncertain.
vocabulary: A couch or carriage carried by attendants, here surrounded by sixty warriors.

notes: The description of the tower’s construction is uncertain; “built in courses” is one understanding of the rare expression.
The verb can suggest looking down from the heights or coming away from them. Lebanon and the named peaks remain part of the poem’s landscape.
The Hebrew repeats the closed or locked image with a rare word commonly understood as a spring; some witnesses repeat “garden.”
vocabulary: A term of intimacy in this love poetry. The endearment itself does not establish that the lovers are biological siblings.

notes: The invitation at the end changes its addressees to a group. The text does not identify a separate speaker for it.
The Hebrew says her life went out “when he spoke,” even though the narrative now finds him gone. The draft preserves this difficult sequence.
The guards beat and wound her and take her wrap. Their violence remains explicit within the searching scene.
The final phrase literally evokes being set in fullness; it is often understood as eyes fitting securely in their settings.
vocabulary: An approximate name for the Hebrew gemstone; ancient stone names do not map securely to modern mineral categories.

sections.1: The Beloved Comes to the Garden

notes: This is one of the book’s most difficult lines. It may describe being carried among chariots of noble people, or contain a personal name, Amminadib. The draft preserves the chariot image and marks the uncertainty.
This verse is 7:1 in the Hebrew source. The next thirteen public verses correspond to Hebrew 7:2–14. “Two camps” can also evoke the place name Mahanaim.
vocabulary: A designation whose relation to a place or to Solomon is uncertain; the poem does not explain it.

notes: The Hebrew text used here speaks of “sleepers’ lips.” “Lips and teeth” reflects a different reading. The change to “my beloved” may signal a new speaker within the verse.
“Desire” also occurs in Genesis 3:16 and 4:7. Those connections are worth hearing without making all three relationships identical.
vocabulary: Fragrant plants associated in the ancient world with love and fertility; also named in Genesis 30.

notes: The Hebrew can mean that her mother would teach her or that her beloved would teach her. The choice does not identify a teacher beyond doubt.
The ending of “flame of YAH” can be read as the short divine name, or as an intensifying expression, “a mighty flame.” The draft retains the possible divine name.
Literally, her vineyard is “before me.” The line stresses her own relation to it, in contrast with Solomon’s arrangements; it does not explicitly state a transaction.
vocabulary: An identifying mark of ownership or authority, worn close to the body. Here it becomes an image of enduring attachment.
